claim: FGF22 is a target-derived presynaptic organizer in the mouse hippocampus.
source: Here we show that fibroblast growth factor 22 (FGF22), a target-derived presynaptic organizer in the mouse hippocampus, induces the expression of insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF2) for the stabilization of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by previous work cited throughout the manuscript (Terauchi et al., 2010; 2015).

claim: FGF22 is released from CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: FGF22 is released from CA3 pyramidal neurons and organizes the differentiation of excitatory nerve terminals formed onto them.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous findings (Terauchi et al., 2010).

claim: FGF22 organizes the differentiation of excitatory nerve terminals formed onto CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: FGF22 is released from CA3 pyramidal neurons and organizes the differentiation of excitatory nerve terminals formed onto them.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous research (Terauchi et al., 2010).

claim: Local application of FGF22 on the axons of dentate granule cells induces IGF2 in the DGCs.
source: Local application of FGF22 on the axons of dentate granule cells (DGCs), which are presynaptic to CA3 pyramidal neurons, induces IGF2 in the DGCs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated experimentally in Figure 3F-I using microfluidic chambers.

claim: IGF2 localizes to DGC presynaptic terminals.
source: IGF2, in turn, localizes to DGC presynaptic terminals and stabilizes them in an activity-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4B showing colocalization with synaptophysin-mCherry.

claim: IGF2 stabilizes DGC presynaptic terminals in an activity-dependent manner.
source: IGF2, in turn, localizes to DGC presynaptic terminals and stabilizes them in an activity-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 6 showing that TTX and Kir2.1 block IGF2's synaptogenic function.

claim: IGF2 application rescues presynaptic defects of Fgf22-/- cultures.
source: IGF2 application rescues presynaptic defects of Fgf22-/- cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7A showing rescue of VGLUT1 clustering defects.

claim: IGF2 is dispensable for the initial presynaptic differentiation.
source: IGF2 is dispensable for the initial presynaptic differentiation, but is required for the following presynaptic stabilization both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 8A-B (6DIV) and Figure 9 (P8).

claim: IGF2 is required for presynaptic stabilization both in vitro and in vivo.
source: IGF2 is dispensable for the initial presynaptic differentiation, but is required for the following presynaptic stabilization both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 8C-F (12DIV) and Figure 9 (P14-P29).

claim: Aberrant synaptic connectivity may result in various neurological and psychiatric disorders, such as autism, Fragile X syndrome, epilepsy, and schizophrenia.
source: Proper synapse formation is critical for appropriate brain function; aberrant synaptic connectivity may result in various neurological and psychiatric disorders, such as autism, Fragile X syndrome, epilepsy, and schizophrenia (Banerjee et al., 2014; Casillas-Espinosa et al., 2012; Lisman, 2012; Pfeiffer and Huber, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Synapse formation begins with target recognition by axons, which is followed by synaptic differentiation at the contact sites.
source: Synapse formation begins with target recognition by axons, which is followed by synaptic differentiation at the contact sites.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Synaptic differentiation is regulated by signals that are exchanged between pre- and postsynaptic sites.
source: Synaptic differentiation is regulated by signals that are exchanged between pre- and postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by extensive literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Various target-derived presynaptic organizers promote local differentiation of presynaptic terminals.
source: Various target-derived presynaptic organizers, such as fibroblast growth factors (FGFs), WNTs, neurotrophins, neuroligins, Ephs/ephrins, SynCAMs, netrin-G ligands (NGLs), and signal regulatory proteins (SIRPs) are shown to promote local differentiation of presynaptic terminals (Darabid et al., 2014; Fox and Umemori, 2006; Henriquez et al., 2011; Johnson-Venkatesh and Umemori, 2010; Regehr et al., 2009; Salinas, 2012; Shen and Scheiffele, 2010; Siddiqui and Craig, 2011; Toth et al., 2013; Zweifel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Presynaptic stabilization has been shown to require gene expression.
source: Presynaptic stabilization has been shown to require gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by examples from Drosophila NMJ cited in the following sentences.

claim: At the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction, a retrograde signal initiated by Gbb controls presynaptic growth and stabilization through transcriptional regulation in motor neurons.
source: At the Drosophila larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ), a retrograde signal initiated by glass bottom boat (Gbb), the Drosophila homologue of bone morphogenic protein (BMP), controls presynaptic growth and stabilization through transcriptional regulation in motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Aberle et al., 2002; Marqués et al., 2002; McCabe et al., 2003).

claim: Gbb and its receptor are internalized and transported from the nerve terminal to the cell body as a retrograde signal.
source: During this process, Gbb and its receptor are internalized and transported from the nerve terminal to the cell body as a retrograde signal.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Aberle et al., 2002; Marqués et al., 2002; McCabe et al., 2003).

claim: The Gbb retrograde signal activates the transcription factor Mad.
source: This signal then activates a transcription factor, Mothers against decapentaplegic (Mad) (Aberle et al., 2002; Marqués et al., 2002; McCabe et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Activated Mad regulates transcription of genes including Trio and dfmr1.
source: Activated Mad regulates transcription of genes including Trio and dfmr1 (fly homolog of FMR1).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Ball et al., 2010; Nahm et al., 2013).

claim: Trio and dFMR1 play critical roles in modulating actin cytoskeletal dynamics and stabilizing microtubules in the presynaptic motor neurons, leading to presynaptic growth and stabilization.
source: Trio and dFMR1 play critical roles in modulating actin cytoskeletal dynamics and stabilizing microtubules in the presynaptic motor neurons, leading to presynaptic growth and stabilization (Ball et al., 2010; Nahm et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: In the mammalian brain, changes in gene expression as a consequence of axon–dendrite contacts are likely to contribute to presynaptic stabilization.
source: In the mammalian brain, changes in gene expression, as a consequence of axon–dendrite contacts, are also likely to contribute to presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is supported by examples cited in the following sentence.

claim: Expression of genes encoding vesicle proteins increases soon after synaptogenesis begins.
source: For example, expression of genes encoding vesicle proteins increases soon after synaptogenesis begins, and neurons synthesize different isoforms of vesicle proteins before and after their axons contact targets (Campagna et al., 1997; Lou and Bixby, 1995; Plunkett et al., 1998; Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Neurons synthesize different isoforms of vesicle proteins before and after their axons contact targets.
source: For example, expression of genes encoding vesicle proteins increases soon after synaptogenesis begins, and neurons synthesize different isoforms of vesicle proteins before and after their axons contact targets (Campagna et al., 1997; Lou and Bixby, 1995; Plunkett et al., 1998; Sanes and Lichtman, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Synaptic stabilization is influenced by neural activity.
source: In addition, synaptic stabilization is influenced by neural activity (Ackermann et al., 2015; Chia et al., 2013; Dalva et al., 2007; Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Ruthazer and Cline, 2004; Waites et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: FGF22 serves as a target-derived presynaptic organizer in the mouse hippocampus.
source: We have previously found that FGF22 serves as a target-derived presynaptic organizer in the mouse hippocampus, a key brain region associated with learning, memory, emotional processing, and social behavior.
evidence: This is supported by previous work (Terauchi et al., 2010; 2015).

claim: The hippocampus is a key brain region associated with learning, memory, emotional processing, and social behavior.
source: We have previously found that FGF22 serves as a target-derived presynaptic organizer in the mouse hippocampus, a key brain region associated with learning, memory, emotional processing, and social behavior.
evidence: This is established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: FGF22-dependent presynaptic differentiation requires two FGF receptors (FGFR2b and FGFR1b) in dentate granule cells.
source: FGF22-dependent presynaptic differentiation requires two FGF receptors (FGFRs), FGFR2b and FGFR1b, in dentate granule cells (DGCs), the major presynaptic neurons for CA3 pyramidal neurons, and the downstream signaling molecules FGFR substrate 2 (FRS2) and PI-3 kinase (Dabrowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FGF22-dependent presynaptic differentiation requires the downstream signaling molecules FRS2 and PI-3 kinase.
source: FGF22-dependent presynaptic differentiation requires two FGF receptors (FGFRs), FGFR2b and FGFR1b, in dentate granule cells (DGCs), the major presynaptic neurons for CA3 pyramidal neurons, and the downstream signaling molecules FGFR substrate 2 (FRS2) and PI-3 kinase (Dabrowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Signals mediated by FRS2 and PI-3 kinase are known to regulate gene expression.
source: Signals mediated by FRS2 and PI-3 kinase are known to regulate gene expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in cell signaling.

claim: Igf2 was one of the most significantly downregulated genes in Fgf22-/- DGCs relative to controls.
source: Microarray analysis revealed several genes that are downregulated in Fgf22-/- DGCs relative to controls (Table 1). One of the most significantly downregulated genes was Igf2.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microarray data shown in Table 1 and confirmed by RT-PCR, qPCR, and in situ hybridization.

claim: Igf2 was decreased to 53.1 ± 12.2% in Fgf22-/- mice relative to WT mice by qPCR.
source: This down-regulation was confirmed by RT-PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), qPCR (Igf2 was decreased to 53.1 ± 12.2% in Fgf22-/- mice relative to WT mice), and in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from qPCR experiments.

claim: At P14, and not at P7, expression of Igf2 mRNA was decreased in DGCs.
source: In situ hybridization experiments showed that at P14, and not at P7, expression of Igf2 mRNA was decreased in DGCs (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization images in Figure 1.

claim: Igf2 expression was not decreased in CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons of Fgf22-/- mice.
source: It was not decreased in other hippocampal cells such as CA1 and CA3 pyramidal neurons of Fgf22-/- mice (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization images in Figure 1.

claim: Igf2 expression was clearly decreased in the inner layer of Fgf22-/- DGCs, where relatively immature DGCs are located.
source: Interestingly, Igf2 expression was clearly decreased in the inner layer of Fgf22-/- DGCs, where relatively immature DGCs are located (Figure 1C and D) (Aguilar-Arredondo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization images in Figure 1C and D, with citation supporting the location of immature DGCs.

claim: DGCs can be classified into several developmental subsets: from newborn to mature, DGCs are positive for Ki67 (dividing DGCs), doublecortin (immature), calretinin (young), and calbindin (mature).
source: Using specific markers, DGCs can be classified into several developmental subsets: from newborn to mature, DGCs are positive for Ki67 (dividing DGCs), doublecortin (immature), calretinin (young), and calbindin (mature) (Abrous et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Ki67-, doublecortin-, and calretinin-positive DGCs populate the inner granule cell layer, and calbindin-positive DGCs the outer.
source: Ki67-, doublecortin-, and calretinin-positive DGCs populate the inner granule cell layer, and calbindin-positive DGCs the outer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DGC organization.

claim: IGF2 protein expression was decreased in calretinin-positive, but not in calbindin-positive DGCs in Fgf22-/- mice relative to WT mice at P14.
source: We found that IGF2 protein expression was decreased in calretinin-positive, but not in calbindin-positive DGCs in Fgf22-/- mice relative to WT mice at P14 (Figure 1G and H; the specificity of the anti-IGF2 antibody was verified using tissues from Igf2-/- mice: Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 1G and H.

claim: No changes in IGF2 expression were observed at P7.
source: Consistent with the in situ results, no changes were observed at P7 (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 1E and F.

claim: The lack of FGF22 impairs IGF2 expression in young, developing DGCs during the stage of synapse stabilization.
source: These results indicate that the lack of FGF22 impairs IGF2 expression in young, developing DGCs during the stage of synapse stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing decreased IGF2 at P14 but not P7, and specifically in calretinin-positive DGCs.

claim: Grik4-Cre mice express Cre in 100% of CA3 pyramidal neurons and 10% of DGCs in the hippocampus.
source: Grik4-Cre mice express Cre in 100% of CA3 pyramidal neurons and 10% of DGCs in the hippocampus (Nakazawa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At P14, IGF2 expression in the inner layer, but not in the outer layer, of DGCs of Fgf22f/f::Grik4-Cre mice was significantly decreased relative to that of control littermates.
source: We found that at P14, IGF2 expression in the inner layer, but not in the outer layer, of DGCs of Fgf22f/f::Grik4-Cre mice was significantly decreased relative to that of control littermates (controls include wild type and Fgf22f/f mice; we did not observe any significant differences in IGF2 staining between wild type and Fgf22f/f mice) (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The level of decrease in IGF2 expression in the inner layer of Fgf22f/f::Grik4-Cre mice was similar to that in Fgf22-/- mice.
source: The level of decrease in IGF2 expression in the inner layer of Fgf22f/f::Grik4-Cre mice was similar to that in Fgf22-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of data from Figure 1 and Figure 2.

claim: CA3-derived FGF22 regulates the expression of IGF2 in young DGCs in vivo.
source: These results suggest that CA3-derived FGF22 regulates the expression of IGF2 in young DGCs in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CA3-selective knockout data in Figure 2.

claim: In hippocampal culture, initial formation of glutamatergic synapses starts from ~3 days in vitro (3DIV), followed by activity-dependent synapse maturation from ~8DIV to ~12DIV.
source: In our hippocampal culture, initial formation of glutamatergic synapses starts from ~3 days in vitro (3DIV), followed by activity-dependent synapse maturation from ~8DIV to ~12DIV (Terauchi et al., 2010; Toth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When cultured hippocampal cells were treated with FGF22 at 1DIV, IGF2 expression in the soma of DGCs was significantly increased at 7DIV.
source: When cultured hippocampal cells were treated with FGF22 at 1DIV, IGF2 expression in the soma of DGCs was significantly increased at 7DIV (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 3A and B.

claim: FGF22-dependent increase in IGF2 was observed in calretinin-positive DGCs, but not in calbindin-positive DGCs.
source: We found that FGF22-dependent increase in IGF2 was observed in calretinin-positive DGCs, but not in calbindin-positive DGCs (Figure 3C and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 3C and E.

claim: IGF2 expression did not increase in non-DGCs, such as CA3 pyramidal neurons, in response to FGF22 treatment.
source: In contrast, IGF2 expression did not increase in non-DGCs, such as CA3 pyramidal neurons, which were identified by immunostaining with Py-antibody (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 3D and E.

claim: FGF22 signaling regulates IGF2 expression in young, calretinin-positive DGCs.
source: These results demonstrate that FGF22 signaling regulates IGF2 expression in young, calretinin-positive DGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing FGF22-induced IGF2 expression specifically in calretinin-positive DGCs.

claim: At 7DIV, a majority of DGCs in culture were calretinin-positive (63.65 ± 1.40%).
source: Note that at 7DIV, a majority of DGCs in culture were calretinin-positive (63.65 ± 1.40%; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that our results with DGCs (identified as Prox1-positive cells) mostly reflect calretinin-positive DGCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Local application of FGF22 at 2DIV to the axonal compartment resulted in an increase in IGF2 level in the cell bodies of Prox1-positive DGCs at 8DIV.
source: Local application of FGF22 at 2DIV to the axonal compartment resulted in an increase in IGF2 level in the cell bodies of Prox1-positive DGCs at 8DIV (Figure 3G–I), indicating that retrograde FGF22 signaling from axon terminals increases IGF2 expression in the soma of DGCs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by microfluidic chamber experiments in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Retrograde FGF22 signaling from axon terminals increases IGF2 expression in the soma of DGCs.
source: Local application of FGF22 at 2DIV to the axonal compartment resulted in an increase in IGF2 level in the cell bodies of Prox1-positive DGCs at 8DIV (Figure 3G–I), indicating that retrograde FGF22 signaling from axon terminals increases IGF2 expression in the soma of DGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the microfluidic chamber experiments showing that axonal FGF22 application increases somal IGF2.

claim: IGF2-EGFP showed a punctate pattern in neurofilament-positive axons of DGCs, while it was dim and diffuse throughout MAP2-positive dendrites of these neurons.
source: IGF2-EGFP showed a punctate pattern in neurofilament-positive axons of DGCs, while it was dim and diffuse throughout MAP2-positive dendrites of these neurons (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 4A.

claim: 83.1 ± 1.0% of IGF2-EGFP puncta were colocalized with synaptophysin-mCherry.
source: IGF2-EGFP puncta in the axons of cultured DGCs were colocalized with cotransfected synaptophysin-mCherry (83.1 ± 1.0% of IGF2-EGFP puncta were colocalized with synaptophysin-mCherry; Figure 4B), indicating that IGF2 localizes to presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: 41.2 ± 0.9% of IGF2-EGFP was localized on the cell surface.
source: We found that 41.2 ± 0.9% of IGF2-EGFP was localized on the cell surface.
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface staining experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: Surface IGF2-EGFP was always colocalized with synaptophysin-mCherry.
source: Surface IGF2-EGFP was always colocalized with synaptophysin-mCherry (Figure 4C), suggesting that IGF2 is secreted and tethered on the surface of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is demonstrated by surface staining experiments in Figure 4C.

claim: IGF2 is secreted and tethered on the surface of presynaptic terminals.
source: Surface IGF2-EGFP was always colocalized with synaptophysin-mCherry (Figure 4C), suggesting that IGF2 is secreted and tethered on the surface of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the surface staining data showing IGF2 on the cell surface at presynaptic terminals.

claim: IGF2R showed a punctate pattern in the axons of DGCs.
source: IGF2R, the major receptor for IGF2 (Fernandez and Torres-Aleman, 2012), showed a punctate pattern in the axons of DGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was localized at presynaptic terminals (84.32 ± 0.90% of IGF2R puncta were colocalized with VGLUT1 puncta; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 84.32 ± 0.90% of IGF2R puncta were colocalized with VGLUT1 puncta.
source: IGF2R, the major receptor for IGF2 (Fernandez and Torres-Aleman, 2012), showed a punctate pattern in the axons of DGCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) and was localized at presynaptic terminals (84.32 ± 0.90% of IGF2R puncta were colocalized with VGLUT1 puncta; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by colocalization analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IGF2 is secreted from the presynaptic terminal and binds to IGF2R, which is also localized at the presynaptic terminal.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that IGF2 is secreted from the presynaptic terminal and binds to IGF2R, which is also localized at the presynaptic terminal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the localization data for IGF2 and IGF2R.

claim: Overexpression of IGF2 increased the density and the size of synaptophysin-YFP puncta in DGCs compared to those in control cultures.
source: Overexpression of IGF2 increased the density and the size of synaptophysin-YFP puncta in DGCs compared to those in control cultures (Figure 5A), without apparently altering the morphology of DGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpression of IGF2 did not apparently alter the morphology of DGCs.
source: Overexpression of IGF2 increased the density and the size of synaptophysin-YFP puncta in DGCs compared to those in control cultures (Figure 5A), without apparently altering the morphology of DGCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by morphological analysis in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No effect of IGF2 overexpression was found in synaptophysin-YFP puncta in Prox1-negative non-DGCs.
source: No effect of IGF2 overexpression was found in synaptophysin-YFP puncta in Prox1-negative non-DGCs (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 5B.

claim: IGF2 promotes presynaptic development specifically in DGCs.
source: These results indicate that IGF2 promotes presynaptic development specifically in DGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing IGF2 effects in DGCs but not non-DGCs.

claim: Blockade of neural activity with tetrodotoxin (TTX) did not disturb the ability of FGF22 to increase IGF2 expression.
source: With FGF22 treatment, IGF2 expression increased in the soma of cultured DGCs (Figure 3A, Figure 6A and B). Blockade of neural activity with tetrodotoxin (TTX) did not disturb the ability of FGF22 to increase IGF2 expression (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data in Figure 6A and B.

claim: TTX treatment reduced the clustering and synaptic localization of IGF2.
source: We then examined the effect of TTX on presynaptic localization of IGF2. We found that TTX treatment reduced the clustering and synaptic localization of IGF2 (Figure 4, Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 6C and D.

claim: The increase in synaptophysin-YFP accumulation by IGF2 overexpression was completely blocked by TTX treatment.
source: Finally, we assessed the requirement of neural activity in IGF2 function to induce presynaptic development. IGF2 overexpression increased synaptophysin-YFP accumulation in cultured DGCs (Figure 5A, Figure 6E and F). This increase was completely blocked by TTX treatment (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Neural activity is not required for FGF22 to induce IGF2 expression, but is necessary for IGF2 to localize to and organize development of presynaptic terminals.
source: These results indicate that neural activity is not required for FGF22 to induce IGF2 expression, but is necessary for IGF2 to localize to and organize development of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TTX experiments showing differential effects on IGF2 expression versus localization and function.

claim: Kir2.1 expression in DGCs decreased the synaptic localization of IGF2.
source: To confirm that the activity of presynaptic neurons is critical for the localization and function of IGF2, we suppressed intrinsic neuronal excitability of DGCs by sparsely transfecting the inwardly rectifying potassium channel, Kir2.1, in culture (Johnson-Venkatesh et al, 2015). Similarly to the results with TTX, Kir2.1 expression in DGCs decreased the synaptic localization of IGF2 (Figure 6G and H) and completely blocked the synaptogenic function of IGF2 (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Kir2.1 expression completely blocked the synaptogenic function of IGF2.
source: To confirm that the activity of presynaptic neurons is critical for the localization and function of IGF2, we suppressed intrinsic neuronal excitability of DGCs by sparsely transfecting the inwardly rectifying potassium channel, Kir2.1, in culture (Johnson-Venkatesh et al, 2015). Similarly to the results with TTX, Kir2.1 expression in DGCs decreased the synaptic localization of IGF2 (Figure 6G and H) and completely blocked the synaptogenic function of IGF2 (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Intrinsic neuronal excitability of DGCs is required for the presynaptic localization of IGF2 and its synaptogenic function.
source: These results indicate that intrinsic neuronal excitability of DGCs is required for the presynaptic localization of IGF2 and its synaptogenic function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Kir2.1 experiments.

claim: In Fgf22-/- cultures, the accumulation of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles, as assessed by the number and size of VGLUT1 puncta, onto dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons is specifically impaired.
source: Our previous analysis showed that in CA3 of Fgf22-/- mice, synaptic connections are made, but synaptic vesicles fail to appropriately accumulate to the presynaptic terminals (Terauchi et al., 2010). In Fgf22-/- cultures, the accumulation of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles, as assessed by the number and size of VGLUT1 (vesicular glutamate transporter 1) puncta, onto dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons is specifically impaired (Terauchi et al., 2010; also see Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by previous work and demonstrated in Figure 7A.

claim: In WT cultures, bath application of IGF2 increased the clustering of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles on the dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons at 13DIV.
source: In WT cultures, bath application of IGF2 increased the clustering of glutamatergic synaptic vesicles on the dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons at 13DIV (Figure 7A); consistent with this result, IGF2 overexpression increased synaptophysin-YFP puncta in DGCs (Figure 5A, Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 7A.

claim: In Fgf22-/- cultures, IGF2 application rescued the defects in VGLUT1 accumulation.
source: In Fgf22-/- cultures, IGF2 application rescued the defects in VGLUT1 accumulation: the restored number and size of VGLUT1 puncta were comparable to those seen in IGF2-treated WT cultures (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 7A.

claim: IGF2 treatment and deficiency of FGF22 did not alter the clustering of VGAT on the dendrite of CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: IGF2 treatment, as well as deficiency of FGF22, did not alter the clustering of VGAT (vesicular GABA transporter; a marker of GABAergic synaptic vesicles) on the dendrite of CA3 pyramidal neurons, indicating that IGF2 and FGF22 are not involved in inhibitory presynaptic development on CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: IGF2 and FGF22 are not involved in inhibitory presynaptic development on CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: IGF2 treatment, as well as deficiency of FGF22, did not alter the clustering of VGAT (vesicular GABA transporter; a marker of GABAergic synaptic vesicles) on the dendrite of CA3 pyramidal neurons, indicating that IGF2 and FGF22 are not involved in inhibitory presynaptic development on CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect on VGAT clustering.

claim: IGF2 treatment and loss of FGF22 did not change the accumulation of postsynaptic markers, PSD95 (glutamatergic) and gephyrin (GABAergic), associated with CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: In addition, IGF2 treatment and loss of FGF22 did not change the accumulation of postsynaptic markers, PSD95 (glutamatergic) and gephyrin (GABAergic), associated with CA3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 7C and D.

claim: IGF2 specifically rescues excitatory presynaptic defects in Fgf22-/- neurons.
source: Altogether, IGF2 specifically rescues excitatory presynaptic defects in Fgf22-/- neurons, suggesting that IGF2 is a mediator of FGF22 signaling to promote excitatory presynaptic development on the dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments showing IGF2 restores VGLUT1 but not VGAT, PSD95, or gephyrin.

claim: IGF2 is a mediator of FGF22 signaling to promote excitatory presynaptic development on the dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Altogether, IGF2 specifically rescues excitatory presynaptic defects in Fgf22-/- neurons, suggesting that IGF2 is a mediator of FGF22 signaling to promote excitatory presynaptic development on the dendrites of CA3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments.

claim: Defects in excitatory synapse formation are observed in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in Fgf22-/- mice as early as P8.
source: Defects in excitatory synapse formation are observed in the CA3 region of the hippocampus in Fgf22-/- mice as early as P8, an early stage of synapse formation (Terauchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: At 6DIV, the basal levels of synaptophysin-YFP accumulation were not different between IGF2-knockdown and control DGCs.
source: At 6DIV, we did not observe any differences between IGF2-knockdown and control DGCs: the basal levels of synaptophysin-YFP accumulation were not different, and IGF2-knockdown DGCs still responded to FGF22 treatment to increase the accumulation of synaptophysin-YFP (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8A and B.

claim: At 6DIV, IGF2-knockdown DGCs still responded to FGF22 treatment to increase the accumulation of synaptophysin-YFP.
source: At 6DIV, we did not observe any differences between IGF2-knockdown and control DGCs: the basal levels of synaptophysin-YFP accumulation were not different, and IGF2-knockdown DGCs still responded to FGF22 treatment to increase the accumulation of synaptophysin-YFP (Figure 8A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8A and B.

claim: At 12DIV, the number and size of synaptophysin-YFP puncta were significantly decreased in IGF2-knockdown DGCs compared to those in controls.
source: On the other hand, at 12DIV, the number and size of synaptophysin-YFP puncta were significantly decreased in IGF2-knockdown DGCs compared to those in controls (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8C and D.

claim: At 12DIV, IGF2-knockdown DGCs no longer show FGF22-dependent increases in the accumulation of synaptophysin-YFP.
source: In addition, IGF2-knockdown DGCs no longer show FGF22-dependent increases in the accumulation of synaptophysin-YFP (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8C and D.

claim: IGF2 is not necessary for the initial presynaptic differentiation induced by FGF22, but is required for a later stage of presynaptic development.
source: These results suggest that IGF2 is not necessary for the initial presynaptic differentiation induced by FGF22, but is required for a later stage of presynaptic development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of IGF2 knockdown at 6DIV versus 12DIV.

claim: IGF2 knockdown from 6DIV decreased the number and size of presynaptic terminals at 12DIV.
source: To confirm the role of IGF2 in the late stage of presynaptic development, we knocked down IGF2 from 6DIV and assessed presynaptic development at 12DIV. IGF2 knockdown from 6DIV decreased the number and size of presynaptic terminals (as assessed by synaptophysin-YFP accumulation) and blocked the synaptogenic effects of FGF22 at 12DIV (Figure 8E and F), suggesting that IGF2 is indeed critical for the later stage of presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8E and F.

claim: IGF2 knockdown from 6DIV blocked the synaptogenic effects of FGF22 at 12DIV.
source: To confirm the role of IGF2 in the late stage of presynaptic development, we knocked down IGF2 from 6DIV and assessed presynaptic development at 12DIV. IGF2 knockdown from 6DIV decreased the number and size of presynaptic terminals (as assessed by synaptophysin-YFP accumulation) and blocked the synaptogenic effects of FGF22 at 12DIV (Figure 8E and F), suggesting that IGF2 is indeed critical for the later stage of presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 8E and F.

claim: IGF2 is critical for the later stage of presynaptic stabilization.
source: To confirm the role of IGF2 in the late stage of presynaptic development, we knocked down IGF2 from 6DIV and assessed presynaptic development at 12DIV. IGF2 knockdown from 6DIV decreased the number and size of presynaptic terminals (as assessed by synaptophysin-YFP accumulation) and blocked the synaptogenic effects of FGF22 at 12DIV (Figure 8E and F), suggesting that IGF2 is indeed critical for the later stage of presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the late knockdown experiments.

claim: In the hippocampus, synapse development from P0 to ~P14 is not apparently influenced by neural activity.
source: In the hippocampus, synapse development from P0 to ~P14 is not apparently influenced by neural activity ("initial synapse differentiation"), but that from ~P14 to ~P28 is regulated by activity, where activity-dependent synapse maturation (e.g., Toth et al., 2013) and activity-dependent synapse elimination (Yasuda et al., 2011) take place.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synapse development from ~P14 to ~P28 is regulated by activity, where activity-dependent synapse maturation and activity-dependent synapse elimination take place.
source: In the hippocampus, synapse development from P0 to ~P14 is not apparently influenced by neural activity ("initial synapse differentiation"), but that from ~P14 to ~P28 is regulated by activity, where activity-dependent synapse maturation (e.g., Toth et al., 2013) and activity-dependent synapse elimination (Yasuda et al., 2011) take place.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At P8, clustering of VGLUT1 in CA3 of Igf2-/- mice was similar to that of WT mice.
source: We found that at P8, clustering of VGLUT1 in CA3 of Igf2-/- mice was similar to that of WT mice (Figure 9A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 9A-D.

claim: At P14, Igf2-/- mice still had a similar number of VGLUT1 puncta, but their size was smaller in the CA3 stratum lucidum region.
source: At P14, Igf2-/- mice still had a similar number of VGLUT1 puncta, but their size was smaller in the CA3 stratum lucidum (SL) region, where the axons of DGCs form excitatory synapses with CA3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 9B.

claim: At P21 and P29, Igf2-/- mice showed a significant decrease in the number and size of VGLUT1 puncta in the SL layer.
source: At P21 and P29, Igf2-/- mice showed a significant decrease in the number and size of VGLUT1 puncta in the SL layer (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 9A-C.

claim: The targeting of DGC axons to CA3 appeared normal in Igf2-/- mice.
source: The targeting of DGC axons to CA3 appeared normal in Igf2-/- mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calbindin staining in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: No defects were observed in the CA3 stratum radiatum region throughout the time periods examined in Igf2-/- mice.
source: No defects were observed in the CA3 stratum radiatum (SR) region, where CA3 to CA3 synapses are located, throughout the time periods we examined (Figure 9A and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 9A and D.

claim: IGF2 is critical for a later stage (after P14) of DGC–CA3 synapse development, but not for CA3–CA3 synapse development.
source: These results suggest that IGF2 is critical for a later stage (after P14) of DGC–CA3 synapse development, but not for CA3–CA3 synapse development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal and spatial pattern of defects in Igf2-/- mice.

claim: In the presynaptic terminals in the SL layer of Igf2-/- mice, there were fewer synaptic vesicles, less clustering of synaptic vesicles, fewer docked vesicles, and smaller synaptic vesicles relative to WT mice.
source: In the presynaptic terminals in the SL layer of Igf2-/- mice, there were fewer synaptic vesicles, less clustering of synaptic vesicles, fewer docked vesicles, and smaller synaptic vesicles relative to WT mice (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis in Figure 10A and B.

claim: No structural defects were found in the SR layer of Igf2-/- mice.
source: In contrast, no structural defects were found in the SR layer of Igf2-/- mice (Figure 10C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy analysis in Figure 10C and D.

claim: In Igf2-/- mice, synaptic vesicles were not stabilized/maintained in the presynaptic terminals specifically at the DGC–CA3 synapses.
source: Together with the immunostaining results (Figure 9), our results suggest that in Igf2-/- mice, synaptic vesicles were not stabilized/maintained in the presynaptic terminals specifically at the DGC–CA3 synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electron microscopy and immunostaining data.

claim: The frequency but not the amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) was significantly decreased in CA3 pyramidal neurons of adult Igf2-/- mice.
source: The frequency but not the amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) was significantly decreased in CA3 pyramidal neurons of adult Igf2-/- mice (Figure 11A and B), suggesting that loss of IGF2 has a prolonged impact on excitatory presynaptic function, without significantly affecting postsynaptic function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 11A and B.

claim: Loss of IGF2 has a prolonged impact on excitatory presynaptic function, without significantly affecting postsynaptic function.
source: The frequency but not the amplitude of miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents (mEPSCs) was significantly decreased in CA3 pyramidal neurons of adult Igf2-/- mice (Figure 11A and B), suggesting that loss of IGF2 has a prolonged impact on excitatory presynaptic function, without significantly affecting postsynaptic function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mEPSC data showing decreased frequency but not amplitude.

claim: The fEPSP slope was significantly smaller in Igf2-/- than WT mice for DGC–CA3 responses.
source: The fEPSP slope was significantly smaller in Igf2-/- than WT mice for DGC–CA3 responses (Figure 11C), but not for CA3–CA3 responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 11C.

claim: The fEPSP slope was not different between Igf2-/- and WT mice for CA3–CA3 responses.
source: The fEPSP slope was significantly smaller in Igf2-/- than WT mice for DGC–CA3 responses (Figure 11C), but not for CA3–CA3 responses.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 11C.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation at DGC–CA3, but not CA3–CA3, synapses was decreased in Igf2-/- mice relative to WT mice.
source: Paired-pulse facilitation at DGC–CA3, but not CA3–CA3, synapses was decreased in Igf2-/- mice relative to WT mice (Figure 11D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data in Figure 11D.

claim: Excitatory synaptic transmission at DGC–CA3 synapses is specifically impaired in Igf2-/- mice due to the loss of synaptic vesicles from the presynaptic terminals.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that excitatory synaptic transmission at DGC–CA3 synapses is specifically impaired in Igf2-/- mice due to the loss of synaptic vesicles from the presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiology and electron microscopy data.

claim: Target-derived FGF22 induces the presynaptic expression of IGF2, and IGF2 in turn, localizes to the presynaptic terminals in an activity-dependent manner for their stabilization.
source: Together, we propose a novel, activity-dependent feedback signaling pathway for presynaptic stabilization in the mammalian brain: target-derived FGF22 induces the presynaptic expression of IGF2, and IGF2 in turn, localizes to the presynaptic terminals in an activity-dependent manner for their stabilization (Figure 12).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarized in the model in Figure 12.

claim: In Drosophila motor neurons, target-derived Gbb signaling induces the expression of Trio in the presynaptic neurons; Trio is then transported back to the nerve terminal and stabilizes cytoskeletal structures of nerve terminals.
source: In Drosophila motor neurons, target-derived Gbb signaling induces the expression of Trio in the presynaptic neurons; Trio is then transported back to the nerve terminal and stabilizes cytoskeletal structures of nerve terminals (Ball et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Gene expression is one of the most significant outcomes of FGF signaling.
source: We focused on FGF signaling, because gene expression is one of the most significant outcomes of FGF signaling (Dorey and Amaya, 2010; Partanen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 often acts as an autocrine factor.
source: IGF2, which often acts as an autocrine factor (Pollak et al., 2004), mediates its functions mainly via IGF2 receptor (IGF2R) as well as via IGF1 receptor (IGF1R) (Fernandez and Torres-Aleman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 mediates its functions mainly via IGF2 receptor (IGF2R) as well as via IGF1 receptor (IGF1R).
source: IGF2, which often acts as an autocrine factor (Pollak et al., 2004), mediates its functions mainly via IGF2 receptor (IGF2R) as well as via IGF1 receptor (IGF1R) (Fernandez and Torres-Aleman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In neurons, both IGF2R and IGF1R are used to mediate IGF2 signal and participate in various physiological functions.
source: In neurons, both receptors are used to mediate IGF2 signal and participate in various physiological functions (Agis-Balboa et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2011; Schmeisser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF1R is a receptor tyrosine kinase, which may regulate local translation.
source: IGF1R is a receptor tyrosine kinase, which may regulate local translation, and IGF2R is known to signal through G proteins, which may ultimately affect calcium homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IGF1R signaling.

claim: IGF2R is known to signal through G proteins, which may ultimately affect calcium homeostasis.
source: IGF1R is a receptor tyrosine kinase, which may regulate local translation, and IGF2R is known to signal through G proteins, which may ultimately affect calcium homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IGF2R signaling.

claim: Calcium homeostasis and local translation of synaptic proteins, as well as regulation of cytoskeletal structures may all contribute to IGF2-dependent presynaptic stabilization.
source: Calcium homeostasis and local translation of synaptic proteins, as well as regulation of cytoskeletal structures like Trio may all contribute to IGF2-dependent presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of IGF2 action.

claim: Active synapses are stabilized and inactive ones are destabilized.
source: It has been proposed that active synapses are stabilized and inactive ones are destabilized (Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Ruthazer and Cline, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In most cases, synaptic transmission and synaptic competition are considered critical for synapse refinement.
source: Various forms of activity are involved: in most cases, synaptic transmission and synaptic competition are considered critical for synapse refinement (Lichtman and Colman, 2000; Waites et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Intrinsic activity plays critical roles in synapse development.
source: In addition, intrinsic activity also plays critical roles in synapse development (Johnson-Venkatesh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity is known to control motor function of KIF proteins and regulate intracellular transport of synaptic components, such as mitochondria and AMPA receptors.
source: Neural activity is known to control motor function of KIF proteins and regulate intracellular transport of synaptic components, such as mitochondria and AMPA receptors (Hoerndli et al., 2015; Saxton and Hollenbeck, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Neural activity modulates phosphorylation of the C terminal domain of KIF3A, which affects loading of N-cadherin containing cargos and contributes to the maintenance of homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: Neural activity also modulates phosphorylation of the C terminal domain of KIF3A, which affects loading of N-cadherin containing cargos and contributes to the maintenance of homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neural activity may regulate the IGF2 transport complex through phosphorylation of motor proteins.
source: Thus, neural activity may regulate the IGF2 transport complex through phosphorylation of motor proteins.
evidence: This is speculation based on known mechanisms of activity-dependent transport regulation.

claim: Neural activity controls exocytotic secretion of cytoplasmic vesicles in neurons.
source: In addition, neural activity may regulate the secretion of IGF2. Neural activity controls exocytotic secretion of cytoplasmic vesicles in neurons: in olfactory bulb neurons, K+-induced depolarization activates the exocytotic Ca2+-sensor, synaptotagmin-10, to induce secretion of IGF1 (Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In olfactory bulb neurons, K+-induced depolarization activates the exocytotic Ca2+-sensor, synaptotagmin-10, to induce secretion of IGF1.
source: In addition, neural activity may regulate the secretion of IGF2. Neural activity controls exocytotic secretion of cytoplasmic vesicles in neurons: in olfactory bulb neurons, K+-induced depolarization activates the exocytotic Ca2+-sensor, synaptotagmin-10, to induce secretion of IGF1 (Cao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Secretion of IGF2 at presynaptic sites might be controlled by neural activity.
source: Thus, in addition to transportation, secretion of IGF2 at presynaptic sites might also be controlled by neural activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to IGF1 secretion.

claim: IGF2 is implicated in maintenance and expansion of neural stem cells.
source: For neurogenesis, IGF2 is implicated in maintenance and expansion of neural stem cells (Ziegler et al., 2012; 2014) and proliferation of neuronal progenitor cells (Burns and Hassan, 2001; Lehtinen et al., 2011) in the developing brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 contributes to proliferation of neuronal progenitor cells in the developing brain.
source: For neurogenesis, IGF2 is implicated in maintenance and expansion of neural stem cells (Ziegler et al., 2012; 2014) and proliferation of neuronal progenitor cells (Burns and Hassan, 2001; Lehtinen et al., 2011) in the developing brain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 contributes to adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the hippocampus.
source: IGF2 also contributes to adult neurogenesis in the subgranular zone of the hippocampus (Bracko et al., 2012; Ouchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 leads to nerve sprouting.
source: For neuronal development, IGF2 leads to nerve sprouting (Caroni and Grandes, 1990), neurite outgrowth (Jeong et al., 2013), as well as spine maturation in cultured hippocampal neurons (Schmeisser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IGF2 promotes neurite outgrowth.
source: For neuronal development, IGF2 leads to nerve sprouting (Caroni and Grandes, 1990), neurite outgrowth (Jeong et al., 2013), as well as spine maturation in cultured hippocampal neurons (Schmeisser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IGF2 promotes spine maturation in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: For neuronal development, IGF2 leads to nerve sprouting (Caroni and Grandes, 1990), neurite outgrowth (Jeong et al., 2013), as well as spine maturation in cultured hippocampal neurons (Schmeisser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IGF2 may serve as a general regulator of the development of presynaptic neurons (DGCs) downstream of FGF22.
source: Thus, IGF2 may serve as a general regulator of the development of presynaptic neurons (DGCs) downstream of FGF22.
evidence: This is speculation based on the broad functions of IGF2.

claim: IκB induces expression of IGF2 for spine maturation in mature hippocampal neurons.
source: Indeed, IκB, which is not utilized by FGF22 signaling, has been shown to induce expression of IGF2 for spine maturation in mature hippocampal neurons (Schmeisser et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The expression of the mouse Igf2 gene is regulated by three alternative promoters.
source: The expression of the mouse Igf2 gene is regulated by three alternative promoters (Sasaki et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Different signals are used to regulate distinct phases of neuronal development.
source: Thus, different signals seem to be used to regulate distinct phases of neuronal development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of multiple pathways regulating IGF2 expression.

claim: Calretinin-positive DGCs elongate axons to CA3 and contact CA3 pyramidal neurons to form synapses.
source: Calretinin-positive DGCs elongate axons to CA3 and contact CA3 pyramidal neurons to form synapses (Aguilar-Arredondo et al., 2015; Li et al., 2009; Ming and Song, 2005; Yasuda et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 is induced by CA3-derived FGF22 when DGC axons contact with their target dendrites.
source: Our results are consistent with the idea that IGF2 is induced by CA3-derived FGF22 when DGC axons contact with their target dendrites.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CA3-selective knockout and local application experiments.

claim: Fgf22-/- mice show defects in excitatory synapse formation both in the SL (where DGC to CA3 synapses are located) as well as SR (where CA3 to CA3 synapses are located).
source: Since Fgf22-/- mice show defects in excitatory synapse formation both in the SL (where DGC to CA3 synapses are located) as well as SR (where CA3 to CA3 synapses are located) (Terauchi et al., 2010), the lack of IGF2 induction in CA3 neurons indicates that IGF2 is a unique target of FGF22 specifically in differentiating DGCs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IGF2 is a unique target of FGF22 specifically in differentiating DGCs.
source: Since Fgf22-/- mice show defects in excitatory synapse formation both in the SL (where DGC to CA3 synapses are located) as well as SR (where CA3 to CA3 synapses are located) (Terauchi et al., 2010), the lack of IGF2 induction in CA3 neurons indicates that IGF2 is a unique target of FGF22 specifically in differentiating DGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cell-type specific induction of IGF2 by FGF22.

claim: CA3 neurons may express genes other than IGF2 in an FGF22-dependent manner for presynaptic stabilization.
source: It is possible that CA3 neurons express genes other than IGF2 in an FGF22-dependent manner for presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms in CA3 neurons.

claim: Different types of presynaptic neurons might process FGF22 signaling through their own transcription regulation to promote neuron type-specific presynaptic stabilization.
source: If so, different types of presynaptic neurons might process FGF22 signaling through their own transcription regulation to promote neuron type-specific presynaptic stabilization.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms of cell-type specificity.

claim: FGF22 affects synapse formation in the SR and SL layers of CA3, but not the SLM (stratum lacunosum moleculare) layer.
source: FGF22 affects synapse formation in the SR and SL layers of CA3, but not the SLM (stratum lacunosum moleculare) layer (Terauchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neuroligins in cerebellar Purkinje cells have a role in the formation of climbing fiber synapses, but not parallel-fiber synapses.
source: Neuroligins in cerebellar Purkinje cells have a role in the formation of climbing fiber synapses, but not parallel-fiber synapses (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cadherin-9 is involved in the formation and differentiation of DGC–CA3 synapses, but not CA3–CA3 synapses.
source: Cadherin-9 is involved in the formation and differentiation of DGC–CA3 synapses, but not CA3–CA3 synapses (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Neuroligin2 regulates inhibitory synaptic function in a pathway-specific manner.
source: Neuroligin2 regulates inhibitory synaptic function in a pathway-specific manner (Gibson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: There are input specific synaptic organizers that cooperate to establish precise networks in the brain.
source: Thus, it appears that there are input specific synaptic organizers that cooperate to establish precise networks in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on examples of input-specific synapse organizers.

claim: In CA3, FGF7 acts as a target-derived presynaptic organizing molecule for inhibitory synapses.
source: In CA3, FGF7 acts as a target-derived presynaptic organizing molecule for inhibitory synapses (Terauchi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FGF22 and FGF7 may regulate distinct molecules in excitatory (DGCs) vs. inhibitory neurons for synapse stabilization.
source: Our preliminary screen suggests that FGF22 and FGF7 may regulate distinct molecules in excitatory (DGCs) vs. inhibitory neurons for synapse stabilization, because Igf2 was not identified as a target gene of FGF7.
evidence: This is an inference based on preliminary screening data.

claim: IGF2 is implicated in behavioral phenotypes such as fear extinction.
source: IGF2 is implicated in behavioral phenotypes such as fear extinction (Agis-Balboa et al., 2011; Agis-Balboa and Fischer, 2014), depression (Luo et al., 2015), and memory consolidation and enhancement in rodents (Chen et al., 2011; Pascual-Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IGF2 is implicated in depression.
source: IGF2 is implicated in behavioral phenotypes such as fear extinction (Agis-Balboa et al., 2011; Agis-Balboa and Fischer, 2014), depression (Luo et al., 2015), and memory consolidation and enhancement in rodents (Chen et al., 2011; Pascual-Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IGF2 is implicated in memory consolidation and enhancement in rodents.
source: IGF2 is implicated in behavioral phenotypes such as fear extinction (Agis-Balboa et al., 2011; Agis-Balboa and Fischer, 2014), depression (Luo et al., 2015), and memory consolidation and enhancement in rodents (Chen et al., 2011; Pascual-Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Administration of IGF2 rescues spine formation and excitatory synaptic function in the hippocampus of a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Administration of IGF2 rescues spine formation and excitatory synaptic function in the hippocampus of a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (Pascual-Lucas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Igf2-/- mice are resistant to acquiring epileptiform events in response to kainate administration.
source: In addition, Igf2-/- mice are resistant to acquiring epileptiform events in response to kainate administration (Dikkes et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fgf22-/- mice show seizure resistant phenotype.
source: Interestingly, Fgf22-/- mice show seizure resistant phenotype (Terauchi et al., 2010) and depression-like behavior (Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Fgf22-/- mice show depression-like behavior.
source: Interestingly, Fgf22-/- mice show seizure resistant phenotype (Terauchi et al., 2010) and depression-like behavior (Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Defects in synapse stabilization through the FGF22–IGF2 pathway may be involved in diseases like epilepsy and depression.
source: Thus, defects in synapse stabilization through the FGF22–IGF2 pathway may be involved in diseases like epilepsy and depression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the behavioral phenotypes of Fgf22-/- and Igf2-/- mice.
